title: Study on wear performance of a novel high-carbon medium manganese bimetal composite using in mining facilities
abstract: Abstract A pin-on-disc tribological test was employed to investigate the self-strengthening effect on the wear performance of a novel Mn8/SS400 bimetal composite. Accelerated wear tests were conducted under normal loads of 20, 60, and 100 N. The results indicate that the increased loads expedite the formation of the hardened layer, augmenting the surface hardness of the Mn8 layer. Once this layer is established, wear rate increment stabilisation occurs, with a 17% reduction observed at 100 N compared to 20 N. The primary strengthening mechanisms primarily involve dislocation and twinning, with no evidence of martensitic transformation or fine grain strengthening. The development of the novel Mn8/SS400 bimetal composites addresses the limited research on high-carbon medium manganese steels. This composite combines the wear resistance of manganese steel with the cost-effectiveness of mild steel, making it suitable for mining applications. By evaluating the self-strengthening mechanisms and durability, the research provides innovative insights into the feasibility of using bimetal materials in mining equipment, addressing the demands for enhanced wear resistance and cost efficiency.
journal: The International Journal of Advanced Manufacturing Technology

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Bimetal composites have gained significant attention due to their favourable combination of mechanical properties and cost-effectiveness compared to single-layer steels [ 1 ]. Extensive research has explored their formation, hot forming, and wear performance to expand their applications [ 2 ,  3 – 4 ]. The properties of these composites are shaped by both inherent characteristics and external environmental factors. The Mn8/SS400 bimetal composite, consisting of high-carbon medium manganese steel (MMSs, i.e., Mn8) and mild steel (SS400), is manufactured through hot roll bonding. This composite combines the wear resistance of MMSs with the weldability and economic benefits of carbon steel substrates, making it a promising material for industrial applications.

MMSs are renowned for demonstrating Twinning-Induced Plasticity (TWIP) and Transformation-Induced Plasticity (TRIP) effects [ 5 ,  6 ,  7 – 8 ], which contribute to a self-strengthening mechanism that enhances surface hardness and improves wear resistance [ 9 ,  10 – 11 ]. These properties make MMSs ideal for wear-resistant applications, particularly in mining. High carbon content further stabilises austenite, allowing it to be retained at room temperature [ 12 ,  13 – 14 ]. Therefore, high-carbon MMSs may present different mechanical and wear properties compared to conventional MMSs. While various studies have explored the mechanical [ 15 ,  16 ,  17 – 18 ] and wear properties [ 19 ,  20 ] of MMSs, research specifically focusing on high-carbon MMSs is limited. Cai et al. [ 21 ] demonstrated that titanium (Ti) additions refine grain structure and induce precipitation strengthening, thereby enhancing hardness and wear resistance. Similarly, higher manganese (Mn) content has been shown to increase tensile strength and impact resistance [ 22 ]. However, the effects of wear under various normal loads on high-carbon MMSs remain inadequately explored. Moreover, studies on polymer and metal-based composites, such as HDPE hybrids and carbon steel, highlight that wear resistance can be significantly improved through the incorporation of reinforcements or by altering external parameters like fluid viscosity and particle impaction angles [ 23 ,  24 – 25 ]. These findings underscore the importance of optimising material properties and environmental conditions to enhance wear performance.

Mining equipment requires exceptional wear resistance due to harsh operating conditions. This is particularly critical for scraper conveyors, where chute wear can lead to operational disruptions, unplanned downtime, and increased maintenance costs. Furthermore, wear-induced surface degradation elevates frictional resistance, leading to higher energy demands in the drive system to maintain operational efficiency. Addressing these challenges underscores the necessity of developing advanced wear-resistant materials, such as the Mn8/SS400 bimetal composite, to mitigate maintenance costs, enhance energy efficiency, and ensure sustainable industrial operations. Although MMSs offer excellent wear resistance, their high cost limits widespread adoption. The Mn8/SS400 bimetal composite presents a cost-effective alternative by combining the wear resistance of Mn8 with the affordability of SS400. Further research is needed to optimise its properties for mining applications.

This research presents a preliminary investigation of high-carbon MMS bimetal composites, focusing on the wear performance analysis of the Mn8 layer. A pin-on-disc tribological test method was employed to simulate the practical conditions of the scraper conveyor, with the scraper material serving as the pin and the bimetal composite as the disc. The effects of varying normal loads on hardened layer formation were examined. The self-hardening behaviour of the bimetal composite after wear was analysed using theoretical calculations and experimental methods. This study not only examines the wear performance of high-carbon MMSs under different loading conditions but also substantiates the potential application of bimetal composite materials in mining applications.

sections.heading: Materials
paragraphs:
In this study, the Mn8/SS400 bimetal composite was used as the disc material for the pin-on-disc tests. Its chemical composition is listed in Table  1 . The discs for the pin-on-disc tests were machined to a diameter of 50.8 mm and a thickness of 6 mm. The Vickers hardness of the disc material is around 280 HV. The counterpart pins were made of 40Cr steel, measuring φ3.96 mm × 25 mm.

Figure  1  presents a schematic diagram of a scraper conveyor, with the enlarged section on the right illustrating a segment of the middle part. This section serves as the main transport module and is the primary area of focus. In operation, the motor drives the chain, which in turn propels the scraper, resulting in wear between the chain and the chute, as well as between the scraper and the chute. Due to the elevated degree of the chain, the predominant wear occurs between the scraper and the chute. To enhance wear resistance, bimetal composites will be used for the top and bottom chutes, while 40Cr steel, a commonly used scraper material, is selected for the pins. Therefore, bimetal composites and 40Cr steel were selected as the disc and pin, respectively, for this study. Fig. 1 Scraper conveyor schematic diagram

The machined surface of the disc material is shown in Fig.  2 a, exhibiting uniform stripe patterns with minimal adherent cutting debris. The initial crystalline phase of the material was examined using optical microscopy (OM), and its phase composition was further verified by X-ray diffraction (XRD). As depicted in Fig.  2 b and c, the Mn8 layer exhibits a fully austenitic structure, with its high carbon content effectively stabilising austenite at room temperature. Fig. 2 Mn8 layer ( a ) machined surface, ( b)  microstructure, and ( c ) XRD spectrum

sections.heading: Wear test method
paragraphs: Pin-on-disc wear tests were performed using an Rtec MFT-5000 Multi-functional Tribometer, as illustrated in Fig.  3 . Controlled loads in the Z-direction were applied to the pin holder, while load sensors detected forces in the X and Z directions. The sensors of the test equipment are categorised into Z-direction and X-direction. Before testing, the Z-direction sensor was left unloaded, ensuring initial readings fluctuated near 0 N. The X-direction sensor was calibrated using an auxiliary leveling device to maintain the alignment of the loading arm. Once the pin was secured, further adjustments ensured that no unintended forces were exerted outside the X-direction. Additionally, the software’s bias mode enabled the zeroing of sensor readings upon setup completion. Prior to testing, the pins and discs underwent cleaning with an ethanol solution. During the test, the disc rotated counterclockwise while the stationary pin experienced wear. Experimental parameters, including normal load, wear duration, and disc revolutions, were systematically varied to evaluate the material’s wear performance under diverse conditions. In this study, accelerated wear tests were conducted at 100 rpm, with a 20 mm wear track diameter, under normal loads of 20, 60, and 100 N. Fig. 3 Schematic of the pin-on-disc tribometer used for wear tests

To accurately determine the parameters for the wear tests, the contact stress between the scraper and the chute was calculated. The total contact stress for each scraper unit was minimal. Considering the 3.96 mm diameter of the pins used in the tests, the actual load on the scraper is approximately 0.23 N. Given the possibility of ore powders getting trapped between the scraper and the chute, which could increase contact stress, it is feasible to increase the normal load for accelerated wear testing. The maximum wear distance reached 22.5 × 10 3  m. Temperature measurements were conducted on the samples during the wear process using a thermometer. However, no significant trends were observed, and thus, the results are not included in the subsequent analysis.

sections.heading: Characterisation methods
paragraphs: Following the wear test, samples cleaning was conducted using an ethanol solution. The wear areas on the discs were then quantified and analysed individually using a VK-X100 Keyence 3D laser scanning microscope. Each experiment was conducted in triplicate to ensure the result reliability and reproducibility. The wear tracks were further investigated through scanning electron microscopy (SEM), while elemental composition analysis of the sample surfaces was performed using energy-dispersive spectrometry (EDS). Cross-section hardness measurements were carried out using a Matsuzawa Via-F automatic Vickers hardness tester. Additionally, after polishing, geometrically necessary dislocation (GND) and phase composition in the cross-sections of the samples were analysed by electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD), employing a 2 µm step size with a scanning area of 250 × 250 µm 2 .

sections.heading: Wear characteristics
paragraphs: To explore the impact of various normal loads on the material’s wear performance, accelerated wear tests were conducted at loads of 20, 60, and 100 N. The wear area and depth under various parameters were quantified using a 3D laser scanning microscope. The wear areas at varying wear distances under different loading forces are depicted in Fig.  4 a–l, while Fig.  4  m presents a 3D profile image of the wear track, allowing measurement of both wear depth and worn area. Figure  4 n displays wear tracks after distances of 3.25 × 10 3  m and 22.5 × 10 3  m under various loading conditions to highlight the observed wear behaviour. Results show that the smallest wear area (6955.78 μm 2 ) occurs under a 20 N load after 3.25 × 10 3  m (20/3.25). In contrast, the largest wear area (43,891.19 μm 2 ) is observed under a 100 N load after 22.5 × 10 3  m (100/22.5). The 3D profile images of the disc wear areas reveal that higher normal loads result in increased wear areas. For example, at a wear distance of 22.5 × 10 3  m, the wear area at 100 N is 53% larger than that at 60 N and 267% larger than that at 20 N. Meanwhile, a sustained wear distance at a constant normal load is observed to coincide with larger wear areas. Notably, smoother wear tracks were observed under 60 N and 100 N at 22.5 × 10 3  m. In contrast, conditions deviating from these parameters showed a greater wear fluctuation, characterised by the formation of irregularly spalled craters during the wear process, suggesting an accelerated wear rate. Fig. 4 (a – d)  Wear area of 3.25, 7.5, 15, 22.5 × 103 m under a normal load of 20 N; ( e–h)  wear area of 3.25, 7.5, 15, 22.5 × 103 m under 60 N; ( i – l)  wear area of 3.25, 7.5, 15, 22.5 × 103 m under 100 N; ( m)  3D profile images and ( n ) 2D wear-track profiles

The wear rate results, calculated using Eq. ( 1 ), are presented in Fig.  5 . These results demonstrate that during the initial 3.25 × 10 3  m of the wear process, the wear rate exhibits significant variability before stabilising. Figure  5 a shows that during the initial wear period of 3.25 × 10 3  m, the wear rate experiences a notable increase to 347.75 μm 2 /N under a normal load of 20 N. Comparatively, the wear rates at 60 N and 100 N are 137.43 μm 2 /N and 103.43 μm 2 /N, respectively, indicating a smaller difference between these higher loads. Specifically, the wear rate at 20 N is 153% higher than that at 60 N and 236% higher than that at 100 N, demonstrating an inverse relationship between the load and wear rate. Figure  5 b further illustrates that higher loads lead to lower initial wear rates, likely due to the immediate plastic deformation induced by higher normal loads, resulting in the rapid formation of a hardened layer [ 34 ,  35 ]. In MMSs, wear behaviour is largely dictated by this hardened layer [ 17 ,  36 ], which increases material hardness and thereby enhances wear resistance. Additionally, as the wear distance increases under a constant load, the rate of wear increment decreases. At 100 N, the incremental wear rate decreases gradually with each successive 7.5 × 10 3  m increase: starting from 194.62 μm 2 /N initially, then reducing to 123.18 μm 2 /N, and further to 121.11 μm 2 /N. This pattern illustrates a decreasing wear rate increment over increasing wear distances. This trend highlights the progressive formation of a hardened layer, a characteristic feature of high-carbon MMSs. Fig. 5 (a)  The wear rate and ( b ) the wear rate increment of discs under different wear conditions

Figure  6  presents the coefficient of friction (COF) curves over 1800s, highlighting the stabilisation times during the running-in phase: approximately 350 s for a 100 N load, 450 s for 60 N, and 500 s for 20 N. This suggests that higher normal loads accelerate the wear process and promote the earlier formation of a hardened layer, leading to faster stabilisation. Generally, the COF correlates with wear rate, where a higher COF corresponds to a higher wear rate [ 37 ]. Under higher loads, COF remains lower during both the running-in and stabilisation phases. Wu et al. reported that appropriate residual stress can reduce the COF during sliding contact by enhancing wear resistance, which decreases the adhesion of abrasives and, consequently, reduces the occurrence of micro-cutting [ 38 ]. During the stable stage, the COF at 20 N is 22% higher than that at 100 N and 10% higher than that at 60 N, suggesting intensified wear at lower loads. This trend aligns with the earlier hardened layer formation at higher loads, which increases material hardness and reduces wear rates. The COF stabilises after an initial running-in period of 500 s, indicating that all wear tests were conducted under steady-state conditions, effectively simulating the operational use of mining facilities. Higher loads accelerate hardened layer formation, reducing wear rates and stabilising COF earlier. This self-hardening effect enhances wear resistance, optimising MMSs for mining applications.
 Fig. 6 The COF curves for wear test at different normal loads

sections.heading: Wear mechanisms
paragraphs: Figure  7  presents SEM micrographs illustrating the sample condition before and after wear. Figure  7 a shows the SEM image of the machined disc without wear, revealing directional cutting marks and minor chips. Figures  7 b–g display post-wear SEM images under various conditions. In Fig.  7 b, the 20/3.25 condition reveals pronounced delamination, with microcracks at pit joints coalescing, leading to severe spalling and fatigue wear [ 21 ,  36 ]. This correlates with the highest wear rate increment in Fig.  5 b, as the material’s low initial hardness prevents early hardened layer formation [ 21 ]. Figure  7 c (20/22.5 condition) shows diminished delamination and increased post-wear debris, with abrasive wear becoming prominent. The wear rate of the material increases uniformly as surface hardness improves due to the hardened layer’s development. At a load of 60 N, initial wear is milder compared to 20 N, with minimal delamination and predominant abrasive wear characterised by ploughed surfaces and spalled fragments. As the wear distance increases, delamination diminishes while debris accumulation rises, consistent with the lower wear rate increments than that at 20 N as shown in Fig.  5 . Under a load of 100 N, initial wear shows significant pits replacing delamination, with increased abrasive content, suggesting a gentler wear process at higher loads. The surface morphology remains unchanged after prolonged wear, suggesting the presence of a hardened layer from the start. Continuous cutting and grooves indicate the persistent involvement of abrasives [ 36 ], aligning with Figs.  5  and  6 , which show a decreasing wear rate and COF at higher loads due to rapid hardened layer formation, enhancing material hardness and reducing wear rate. Figures  7 h–j show EDS spectra at different points: point A represents elemental composition pre-wear, while points B and C represent composition post-wear at the 100/22.5 parameter. EDS analysis reveals significant increases in carbon and oxygen content post-wear, indicating oxide and carbide formation during wear [ 39 ]. However, the content of other elements exhibited minimal variation, suggesting negligible adhesive wear. Higher loads reduce delamination and enhance abrasive wear, promoting hardened layer formation and decreasing wear rates. EDS confirms oxide and carbide formation, with minimal adhesive wear contribution. Fig. 7 The SEM observed under ( a ) as received, ( b)  20/3.25, ( c)  20/22.5, ( d)  60/3.25, ( e)  60/22.5, ( f)  100/3.25, ( g)  100/22.5 and EDS spectra weight percent of ( h ) point A,  i  point B,  j  point C

sections.heading: Self-strengthening mechanisms
paragraphs: To further investigate the wear behaviour of high-carbon MMSs under the operating conditions of mining facilities, this study examines the self-hardening mechanism. Figure  8  shows the hardness of the worn sections under different loading conditions, demonstrating a significant increase in surface hardness after wear. The hardness is highest at the wear surface and decreases with increasing distance from the wear surface, approaching the substrate hardness at approximately 200 µm. This indicates the formation of a hardened layer approximately 200 µm thick from the wear surface. The cross-sectional hardnesses of the material after wear for 22.5 × 10 3  m under different normal loads are shown in Fig.  8 a. These data suggest that, overall, higher normal loads result in higher surface layer hardness for the same wear distance. However, at 20 N, the worn surface hardness is significantly lower (around 320 HV) compared to 60 N and 100 N, aligning with the highest wear rate and severe surface delamination observed. Conversely, the cross-sectional hardness at 60 N shows only a slight reduction compared to 100 N, consistent with their similar wear rates. Figure  8 b illustrates the cross-sectional hardness at different wear distances under a constant 100 N load. Despite minor differences, the hardness of the material remains around 350 HV. Given that the incremental wear rate at 100 N is minimal and only pits form during the initial 3.25 × 10 3  m of wear, it can be concluded that the hardened layer develops early in the wear process and is nearly complete within this distance. The formation of the hardened layer enhances the surface hardness, thereby reducing its wear rate and slowing down the wear process. Fig. 8 Cross-section hardness variations under different ( a ) loads and ( b ) wear distances

In addition to dislocation strengthening, TWIP and TRIP effects have been a focal point of research in MMSs [ 5 ,  21 ]. In most MMSs, two primary strengthening mechanisms occur simultaneously during deformation: the transformation of austenite to martensite phase and the formation of deformation twins. These mechanisms significantly enhance the material’s overall hardness and wear resistance. The formation of martensite increases hardness through phase transformation, while deformation twins create additional barriers to dislocation motion, improving the material’s deformation resistance [ 17 ]. A calculation based on Eq. ( 3 ) yields an SFE value of 23 mJ/m 2  for this high-carbon MMS. Prior studies indicate that when the SFE of MMSs exceeds 18 mJ/m 2 , only the TWIP mechanism is active, and martensitic transformation does not occur [ 41 ]. This suggests that during wear, deformation strengthening in this material arises solely from twinning within the austenite phase, enhancing hardness without martensite formation. TWIP effect is a common deformation strengthening mechanism for high Mn steels, suggesting that the deformation behaviour of high-carbon MMSs aligns more closely with high Mn steels than that of MMSs. This assertion is supported by the phase composition and EBSD diagram in Fig.  10 . After 100/22.5 of wear, only the austenite phase remains, with deformation twins present. This suggests that during the wear process of these high-carbon MMSs, strengthening primarily occurs through dislocation and twinning mechanisms, with no contribution from martensitic transformation. It is noteworthy that the high-carbon MMS formed partial annealing twins after hot rolling, as shown at point A in Fig.  10 c, whereas the deformation twins formed after wear are shown at point B. The two types of twins can be clearly distinguished by morphology. Additionally, although a large number of low-angle grain boundaries were generated on the worn surface, the overall grain diameter remained around 40 μm, indicating no significant fine grain strengthening. Fig. 10 Phase composition and grain boundaries measured by EBSD on ( a ) as received;（ b)  100/22.5 and ( c ) twins observed by EBSD

Figure  11  illustrates the self-hardening mechanism of the MMS layer. During the wear process, the original austenite grains in the MMS layer deform under external forces. Based on prior analyses and SFE calculations, this high-carbon medium manganese steel exhibits significant dislocation activity during wear, with the TWIP effect being the primary strengthening mechanism. Notably, no martensitic phase transformation occurs during wear. Instead, in addition to the original annealed twins, a small number of deformation twins form within the austenite. The accumulated dislocations do not result in grain boundary formation, and consequently, no grain refinement effect is observed. The self-hardening mechanism of high-carbon MMSs is primarily governed by dislocation strengthening and the TWIP effect, with no martensitic transformation observed. Higher loads enhance hardness and wear resistance through increased dislocation density and deformation twinning, leading to stable wear rates. Fig. 11 Self-hardening mechanism of Mn8 layer

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: Accelerated wear tests were evaluated using a pin-on-disc tribological testing method at room temperature under varied conditions to simulate the bimetal composite performance under practical mining facility conditions. The conclusions drawn from this study are outlined below. During the initial stages of wear, higher normal loads expedite the formation of hardened layers. This results in an earlier development of the hardened layer with increasing load, subsequently leading to a diminished wear rate and an accelerated transition to steady wear conditions. After wear, a dislocation layer forms within the high-carbon medium manganese bimetal composite, which enhances surface hardness. Consequently, this impedes the wear process, resulting in a reduction of the wear rate. Upon the formation of the hardened layer, the wear rate stabilises, with higher loads inducing a marginal reduction in the wear rate. This phenomenon arises from the generation of additional dislocations under higher loads, thereby augmenting dislocation strengthening. Martensite formation and fine grain strengthening were absent during the wear of the high-carbon medium manganese bimetal composite. Instead, the observed increase in hardness can be attributed to the emergence of deformation twins and dislocation strengthening. Given the self-strengthening properties of the novel Mn8/SS400 bimetal, its application to mining facilities requiring high wear resistance and cost-efficiency is promising and warrants further investigation.
